subject: Business
title: The Decoy Effect in Pricing
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Decoy Effect in Pricing.

hook.text: The Economist offered: web-only $59, print-only $125, print+web $125. The middle option looks absurd.

buildup.text: That absurd option is the decoy. It exists only to make the combo look like a steal.

discovery.text: Without the decoy, most people chose web-only. With it, most chose the expensive combo.

twist.text: Nobody picks the decoy. Its job is to make another option look comparatively better.

climax.text: SaaS companies use three-tier pricing for this reason. The middle tier is often the decoy.

punchline.text: The option nobody picks is the one doing all the work.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a decoy option in pricing?
options: To make another option seem more attractive by comparison
To increase the number of options available

details.summary: The decoy effect introduces a strategically inferior third option that makes one of the original two options look significantly more attractive. Adding a dominated alternative shifts consumer preference toward the target option without changing the other choices available.
details.whyItMatters: The decoy effect is a proven pricing strategy used by everyone from movie theaters to software companies. Understanding it helps businesses optimize pricing tiers and helps consumers recognize when their preferences are being engineered.
takeaways: A dominated third option shifts preference toward the strategically targeted choice
The decoy is designed to be clearly worse than the target option
Subscription pricing commonly uses decoys to steer toward premium tiers

faq.question: How does a popcorn pricing example demonstrate the decoy effect?
faq.answer: A small popcorn costs three dollars and large costs seven. Few buy the large. Add a medium for six fifty. Now the large seems like a bargain compared to the medium, and large sales increase dramatically. The medium is the decoy making the large appear more attractive.

faq.question: Does the decoy effect work in business-to-business pricing?
faq.answer: Yes. SaaS companies commonly offer three tiers where the middle option makes the premium tier look like better value. Enterprise proposals include a stripped-down option that makes the full package seem reasonable. Professional buyers are susceptible to decoys too.
